Speedy (Snp 4.14 15.1)

They’d not stand for buying and selling;
a mendicant would not speak ill at all.
They wouldn’t linger in the village,
nor cajole people from desire for profit.
Speedy (Snp 4.14 16.1)

A mendicant would be no boaster,
nor would they speak suggestively.
They wouldn’t train in impudence,
nor speak argumentatively.
Speedy (Snp 4.14 17.1)

They wouldn’t be led into lying,
nor be deliberately devious.
And they’d never look down on another
because of livelihood, wisdom, or precepts and vows.
Speedy (Snp 4.14 18.1)

Though provoked from hearing much talk
from ascetics saying all different things,
they wouldn’t react harshly,
for the virtuous do not retaliate.
Speedy (Snp 4.14 19.1)

Having understood this teaching,
inquiring, a mendicant would always train mindfully.
Knowing quenching as peace,
they’d not be negligent in Gotama’s bidding.
Speedy (Snp 4.14 20.1)

For he is the vanquisher, the unvanquished,
seer of the truth as witness, not by legends—
that’s why, being diligent, they would always train
respectfully in the Buddha’s teaching.”
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 1.1)

Peril stems from those who take up arms—
just look how people conflict!
I shall extol how I came to be
stirred with a sense of urgency.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 2.1)

I saw this population flounder,
like a fish in a little puddle.
Seeing them at odds with each other,
fear came upon me.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 3.1)

The world around was volatile,
all directions were in turmoil.
Wanting a home for myself,
I saw nowhere unsettled.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 4.1)

Yet even in their settlement they were at odds—
seeing that, I grew uneasy.
Then I saw a dart there,
so hard to see, stuck in the heart.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 5.1)

When struck by that dart,
you run around in all directions.
But when that same dart has been plucked out,
you neither run around nor sink down.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 6.1)

(On that topic, the trainings are recited.)
Whatever attachments there are in the world,
don’t pursue them.
Having pierced through sensual pleasures in every way,
train yourself for extinguishment.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 7.1)

Be truthful, not rude,
free of deceit, and rid of slander;
without anger, a sage would cross over
the evils of greed and avarice.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 8.1)

Prevail over sleepiness, sloth, and drowsiness,
don’t abide in negligence,
A person intent on quenching
would not stand for arrogance.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 9.1)

Don’t be led into lying,
or get caught up in affection for form.
Completely understand conceit,
and desist from hasty conduct.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 10.1)

Don’t relish the old,
or welcome the new.
Don’t grieve for what is running out,
or get attached to things that pull you in.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 11.1)

Greed, I say, is the great flood,
and longing is the current—
the basis, the compulsion,
the swamp of sensuality so hard to get past.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 12.1)

The sage never strays from the truth;
the brahmin stands on solid ground.
Having given up everything,
they are said to be at peace.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 13.1)

They have truly known, they’re a knowledge master,
understanding the teaching, they are independent.
They rightly proceed in the world,
not coveting anything here.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 14.1)

One who has crossed over sensuality here,
the chain in the world so hard to get past,
grieves not, nor hopes;
they’ve cut the strings, they’re no longer bound.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 15.1)

What came before, let wither away,
and after, let there be nothing.
If you don’t grasp at the middle,
you will live at peace.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 16.1)

One who has no sense of ownership
in the whole realm of name and form,
does not grieve for that which is not,
they suffer no loss in the world.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 17.1)

If you don’t think of anything
as belonging to yourself or others,
not finding any possessiveness,
you won’t grieve, thinking “I don’t have it”.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 18.1)

Not bitter, not fawning,
unstirred, everywhere even;
when asked about one who is unwavering,
I declare that that is the benefit.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 19.1)

For the unstirred who understand,
there’s no performance of deeds.
Desisting from instigation,
they see sanctuary everywhere.
Taking Up Arms (Snp 4.15 20.1)

A sage doesn’t speak of themselves as being
among superiors, inferiors, or equals.
Peaceful, rid of stinginess,
they are neither ditching nor taking up.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 1.1)

“Never before have I seen,” said Venerable Sāriputta,
“or heard from anyone
about a teacher of such graceful speech,
come from Tusita heaven to lead a community.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 2.1)

To all the world with its gods
he appears as a Clear-eyed One
who has dispelled all darkness,
and alone attained to bliss.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 3.1)

On behalf of the many here still bound,
I have come seeking with a question
to that Buddha, unattached and impartial,
free of deceit, come to lead a community.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 4.1)

Suppose a mendicant who loathes attachment
frequents a lonely lodging—
the root of a tree, a charnel ground,
on mountains, or in caves.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 5.1)

In these many different lodgings,
how many dangers are there
at which a mendicant in their silent lodging
ought not tremble?
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 6.1)

On their journey to the untrodden place,
how many adversities are there in the world
that must they overcome
in their remote lodging?
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 7.1)

What ways of speech should they have?
Of what kind is their alms resort?
What precepts and vows
should a resolute mendicant uphold?
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 8.1)

Having undertaken what training,
unified, alert, and mindful,
would they purge their own stains,
like a smith smelting silver?”
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 9.1)

“If one who loathes attachment frequents a lonely lodging,” said the Buddha to Sāriputta,
“in their search for awakening—as accords with the teaching—
I shall tell you, as I understand it,
what is comfortable for them.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 10.1)

An attentive one, a mindful mendicant living on the periphery
should not be afraid of five perils:
flies, mosquitoes, reptiles,
human contact, or four-legged creatures.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 11.1)

Nor should they fear followers of other teachings,
even having seen the many threats they pose.
And then one seeking the good
should overcome any other adversities.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 12.1)

Afflicted by illness and hunger,
they should endure cold and excessive heat.
Though afflicted by many such things, the homeless one
should exert energy, firmly striving.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 13.1)

They must not steal or lie;
and should touch creatures firm or frail with love.
If they notice any clouding of the mind,
they should dispel it as Māra’s ally.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 14.1)

They must not fall under the sway of anger or arrogance;
having dug them out by the root, they would stand firm.
Then, faced with likes and dislikes,
they would surely overcome.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 15.1)

Putting wisdom in the foremost place, rejoicing in goodness,
they would put an end to those adversities.
They’d vanquish discontent in their remote lodging.
And they’d vanquish the four lamentations:
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 16.1)

‘What will I eat? Where will I eat?
Oh, I slept badly! Where will I sleep?’
The trainee, the migrant without abode,
would dispel these lamentable thoughts.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 17.1)

Receiving food and clothes in due season,
they would know moderation for the sake of contentment.
Guarded in these things, walking restrained in the village,
they wouldn’t speak harshly even when provoked.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 18.1)

Eyes downcast, not footloose,
devoted to absorption, they’d be very wakeful.
Grounded in equanimity, serene,
they should cut off worrisome habits of thought.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 19.1)

A mindful one would welcome reproach,
and would dissolve hard-heartedness toward their spiritual companions.
They may utter skillful speech, but not for too long,
and they shouldn’t provoke people to blame.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 20.1)

And there are five more taints in the world,
for the removal of which the mindful one should train,
vanquishing desire for sights,
sounds, flavors, smells, and touches.
With Sāriputta (Snp 4.16 21.1)

Having removed desire for these things,
a mindful mendicant, their heart well freed,
rightly investigating the Dhamma in good time,
at one, would banish the darkness.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 1.1)

From the fair city of the Kosalans
to the southern region
came a brahmin expert in hymns,
aspiring to nothingness.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 2.1)

He settled in a region under the shared dominion
of Assaka and Muḷaka,
where he lived on the bank of the Godāvarī River,
getting by on gleanings and fruit.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 3.1)

He was supported
by a prosperous village nearby.
With the revenue earned from there
he performed a great sacrifice.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 4.1)

When he had completed the great sacrifice,
he returned to his hermitage once more.
Upon his return,
another brahmin arrived.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 5.1)

Foot-sore and thirsty,
with grotty teeth and dusty head,
he approached the other
and asked for five hundred coins.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 6.1)

When Bāvari saw him,
he invited him to sit down,
asked of his happiness and well-being,
and said the following.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 7.1)

“Whatever I had available to give,
I have already distributed.
Believe me, brahmin,
I don’t have five hundred coins.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 8.1)

“If, good fellow, you do not
give me what I ask,
then on the seventh day,
let your head explode in seven!”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 9.1)

After performing a ritual,
that charlatan uttered his dreadful curse.
When he heard these words,
Bāvari became distressed.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 10.1)

Not eating, he grew emaciated,
stricken by the dart of sorrow.
And in such a state of mind,
he could not enjoy absorption.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 11.1)

Seeing him anxious and distraught,
a goddess wishing to help,
approached Bāvari
and said the following.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 12.1)

“That charlatan understands nothing
about the head, he only wants money.
When it comes to heads or head-splitting,
he has no knowledge at all.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 13.1)

“Then you, Madam, must know—
please answer my question.
Let me hear what you say
about heads and head-splitting.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 14.1)

“I too do not know that,
I have no knowledge in that matter.
When it comes to heads or head-splitting,
it is the Victors who have vision.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 15.1)

“So who then,
in all this vast territory,
does know about heads and head-splitting?
Please tell me, goddess.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 16.1)

“From the city of Kapilavatthu
the World Leader has gone forth.
He is a scion of King Okkāka,
a Sakyan, and a beacon.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 17.1)
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 18.1)

That Buddha, the Blessed One in the world,
the Clear-eyed One, teaches Dhamma.
Go to him and ask—
he will answer you.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 19.1)

When he heard the word “Buddha”,
Bāvari was elated.
His sorrow faded,
and he was filled to brimming with joy.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 20.1)

Uplifted, elated, and inspired,
Bāvari questioned that goddess:
“But in what village or town,
or in what land is the protector of the world,
where we may go and pay respects
to the Awakened One, best of men?”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 21.1)

“Near Sāvatthī, home of the Kosalans, is the Victor
abounding in wisdom, vast in intelligence.
That Sakyan is indefatigable, free of defilements,
that captain of men understands head-splitting.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 22.1)

Therefore he addressed his acolytes,
brahmins who had mastered the hymns:
“Come, students, I shall speak.
Listen to what I say.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 23.1)

Today has arisen in the world
one whose appearance in the world
is hard to find again—
he is renowned as the Awakened One.
Quickly go to Sāvatthī
and see the best of men.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 24.1)

“Brahmin, how then are we to know
the Buddha when we see him?
We don’t know, please tell us,
so we can recognize him.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 25.1)

“The marks of a great man
have been handed down in our hymns.
Thirty-two have been described,
complete and in order.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 26.1)

One upon whose body is found
these marks of a great man
has two possible destinies,
there is no third.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 27.1)

If he stays at home,
having conquered this land
without rod or sword,
he shall govern by principle.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 28.1)

But if he goes forth
from the lay life to homelessness,
he becomes an Awakened One, a perfected one,
with veil cast off, supreme.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 29.1)

Ask him about my birth, clan, and marks,
my hymns and acolytes; and further,
about heads and head-splitting—
but do so only in your mind!
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 30.1)

If he is the Buddha
of unhindered vision,
he will answer with his voice
the questions in your mind.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 31.1)

Sixteen brahmin acolytes
heard what Bāvari said:
Ajita, Tissametteyya,
Puṇṇaka and Mettagū,
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 32.1)

Dhotaka and Upasīva,
Nanda and then Hemaka,
both Todeyya and Kappa,
and Jatukaṇṇī the astute,
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 33.1)

Bhadrāvudha and Udaya,
and the brahmin Posāla,
Mogharāja the intelligent,
and Piṅgiya the great seer.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 34.1)

Each of them had their own following,
they were renowned the whole world over.
Those attentive ones, meditators who love absorption,
were redolent with the potential of their past deeds.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 35.1)

Having bowed to Bāvari,
and circled him to his right,
they set out for the north,
with their dreadlocks and hides.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 36.1)

First to Patiṭṭhāna of Muḷaka,
then on to the citadel of Māhissatī;
to Ujjenī and Gonaddhā,
and Vedisa, and Vanasa.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 37.1)

Then to Kosambī and Sāketa,
and the capital city of Sāvatthī;
on they went to Setavyā and Kapilavatthu,
and the homestead at Kusinārā.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 38.1)

To Pāvā they went, and Bhoga City,
and on to Vesālī and the Magadhan city.
Finally they reached the Pāsāṇaka Shrine,
fair and delightful.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 39.1)

Like a thirsty person to cool water,
like a merchant to great profit,
like a heat-struck person to shade,
they quickly climbed the mountain.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 40.1)

At that time the Buddha,
at the fore of the mendicant Saṅgha,
was teaching the mendicants the Dhamma,
like a lion roaring in the jungle.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 41.1)

Ajita saw the Buddha,
like the sun shining with a hundred rays,
like the moon on the fifteenth day
when it has come into its fullness.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 42.1)

Then he saw his body,
complete in all features.
Thrilled, he stood to one side
and asked this question in his mind.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 43.1)
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 44.1)

“His age is a hundred and twenty.
By clan he is a Bāvari.
There are three marks on his body.
He is a master of the three Vedas,
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 45.1)

the teachings on the marks, the testaments,
the vocabularies, and the rituals.
He teaches recitation to five hundred,
and has reached proficiency in his own teaching.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 46.1)

“O supreme man, cutter of craving,
please reveal in detail
Bāvari’s marks—
let us doubt no longer!”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 47.1)
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 48.1)

Hearing the answers
without having heard any questions,
all the people, inspired,
with cupped palms, wondered:
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 49.1)

“Who is it that asked a question with their mind?
Was it a god or divinity?
Or Indra, Sujā’s husband?
To whom does the Buddha reply?”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 50.1)

“Bāvari asks
about heads and head-splitting.
May the Buddha please answer,
and so, O seer, dispel our doubt.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 51.1)

“Know ignorance as the head,
and knowledge as the head-splitter,
when joined with faith, mindfulness, and immersion,
and enthusiasm and energy.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 52.1)

At that, the student,
full of inspiration,
arranged his antelope-skin cloak over one shoulder,
and fell with his head to the Buddha’s feet.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 53.1)

“Good fellow, the brahmin Bāvari
together with his acolytes,
elated and happy,
bows to your feet, O Clear-eyed One!”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 54.1)

“May the brahmin Bāvari be happy,
together with his acolytes.
And may you, too, be happy!
May you live long, student.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 55.1)

To Bāvari and you all
I grant the opportunity to clear up all doubt.
Please ask
whatever you want.”
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 56.1)

Granted the opportunity by the Buddha,
they sat down with cupped palms.
Ajita asked the Realized One
the first question right there.
Introductory Verses (Snp 5.1 56.5)
The introductory verses are finished.
The Questions of Ajita (Snp 5.2 1.1)

“By what is the world shrouded?” said Venerable Ajita.
“Why does it not shine?
Tell me, what is its sullying?
What is its greatest fear?”
The Questions of Ajita (Snp 5.2 2.1)

“The world is shrouded in ignorance.” replied the Buddha.
“Avarice and negligence make it not shine.
Muttered prayer is its sullying, I say.
Suffering is its greatest fear.”
The Questions of Ajita (Snp 5.2 3.1)

“The streams flow everywhere,” said Venerable Ajita.
“What is there to block them?
And tell me the restraint of streams—
by what are they locked out?”
The Questions of Ajita (Snp 5.2 4.1)

“The streams in the world,” replied the Buddha,
“are blocked by mindfulness.
I tell you the restraint of streams—
they are locked out by wisdom.”
The Questions of Ajita (Snp 5.2 5.1)

“That wisdom and mindfulness,” said Venerable Ajita,
“and that which is name and form, good fellow;
when questioned, please tell me of this:
where does this all cease?”
The Questions of Ajita (Snp 5.2 6.1)

“This question which you have asked,
I shall answer you, Ajita.
Where name and form
cease with no residue left behind—
with the cessation of consciousness,
here they cease.”
The Questions of Ajita (Snp 5.2 7.1)

“There are those who have appraised the teaching,
and many kinds of trainees here.
Now you, being alert, are asked
to tell me their behavior, good fellow.”
The Questions of Ajita (Snp 5.2 8.1)

“Not greedy for sensual pleasures,
their mind would be unclouded.
Skilled in all things,
a mendicant would wander mindful.”
The Questions of Tissametteyya (Snp 5.3 1.1)

“Who here in the world is content?” said Venerable Tissametteyya.
“Who has no perturbations?
What thoughtful one, knowing both ends,
is not stuck in the middle?
Who do they say is a great man?
Who here has escaped the seamstress?”
The Questions of Tissametteyya (Snp 5.3 2.1)

“Leading the spiritual life among sensual pleasures,” replied the Buddha,
“rid of craving, ever mindful;
a mendicant who, after appraisal, is quenched:
that’s who has no perturbations.
The Questions of Tissametteyya (Snp 5.3 3.1)

That thoughtful one, knowing both ends,
is not stuck in the middle.
He is a great man, I declare;
he has escaped the seamstress here.”
The Questions of Puṇṇaka (Snp 5.4 1.1)

“To the imperturbable, the seer of the root,” said Venerable Puṇṇaka,
“I have come seeking with a question.
On what grounds have seers and men,
aristocrats and brahmins here in the world
performed so many different sacrifices to the gods?
I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this.”
The Questions of Puṇṇaka (Snp 5.4 2.1)

“Whatever seers and men,” replied the Buddha,
“aristocrats and brahmins here in the world
have performed so many different sacrifices to the gods:
all performed sacrifices bound to old age,
longing for this place.”
The Questions of Puṇṇaka (Snp 5.4 3.1)

“As to those seers and men,” said Venerable Puṇṇaka,
“and aristocrats and brahmins here in the world
who have performed so many different sacrifices to the gods:
being diligent in the technique of sacrifice,
have they crossed over rebirth and old age, good fellow?
I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this.”
The Questions of Puṇṇaka (Snp 5.4 4.1)

“Hoping, invoking, praying, and worshiping,” replied the Buddha,
“they pray for pleasure derived from profit.
Devoted to sacrifice, besotted by rebirth,
they’ve not crossed over rebirth and old age, I declare.”
The Questions of Puṇṇaka (Snp 5.4 5.1)

“If those devoted to sacrifice,” said Venerable Puṇṇaka,
“have not, by sacrificing, crossed over rebirth and old age,
who then in the world of gods and humans
has crossed over rebirth and old age, good fellow?
I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this.”
The Questions of Puṇṇaka (Snp 5.4 6.1)

“Having appraised the world high and low,” replied the Buddha,
“there is nothing in the world that disturbs them.
Peaceful, unclouded, untroubled, with no need for hope—
they’ve crossed over rebirth and old age, I declare.”
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 1.1)

“I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this,” said Venerable Mettagū,
“for I think you are a knowledge master, evolved.
Where do all these sufferings come from,
in all their countless forms in the world?”
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 2.1)

“You have rightly asked me of the origin of suffering,” replied the Buddha,
“I shall tell you as I understand it.
Attachment is the source of suffering
in all its countless forms in the world.
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 3.1)

When an ignorant person builds up attachments,
that dullard returns to suffering again and again.
So let one who understands not build up attachments,
contemplating the inception of suffering and rebirth.”
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 4.1)

“Whatever I asked you have explained to me.
I ask you once more, please tell me this:
How do the attentive cross the flood
of rebirth, old age, sorrow, and lamenting?
Please, sage, answer me clearly,
for truly you understand this matter.”
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 5.1)

“I shall extol a teaching to you,” replied the Buddha,
“that is apparent in the present, not relying on legends.
Having understood it, one who lives mindfully
may cross over clinging in the world.”
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 6.1)

“And I rejoice, great seer,
in that supreme teaching,
having understood which, one who lives mindfully
may cross over clinging in the world.”
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 7.1)

“Once you’ve expelled relishing and dogmatism,” replied the Buddha,
“regarding everything you are aware of—
above, below, all round, between—
having cast aside consciousness, don’t continue in existence.
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 8.1)

A mendicant who wanders meditating like this,
diligent and mindful, calling nothing their own,
would, being wise, give up the suffering
of rebirth, old age, sorrow and lamenting right here.”
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 9.1)

“I rejoice in the words of the great seer!
You have expounded non-attachment well, Gotama.
Clearly the Buddha has given up suffering,
for truly you understand this matter.
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 10.1)

Surely, sage, those you’d regularly instruct
would also give up suffering.
Having met, I bow especially to you, O spiritual giant;
hopefully the Buddha may regularly instruct me.”
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 11.1)

“Any brahmin recognized as a knowledge master,
who has nothing, unattached to sensual life,
clearly has crossed this flood,
crossed to the far shore, kind, wishless.
The Questions of Mettagū (Snp 5.5 12.1)

And a wise person here, a knowledge master,
having untied the bond to life after life,
free of craving, untroubled, with no need for hope,
has crossed over rebirth and old age, I declare.”
The Questions of Dhotaka (Snp 5.6 1.1)

“I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this,” said Venerable Dhotaka,
“I long for your voice, great seer.
After hearing your message,
I shall train myself for extinguishment.”
The Questions of Dhotaka (Snp 5.6 2.1)

“Well then, be keen, alert,” replied the Buddha,
“and mindful right here.
After hearing this message, go on
and train yourself for extinguishment.”
The Questions of Dhotaka (Snp 5.6 3.1)

“I see in the world of gods and humans
a brahmin traveling with nothing.
I bow especially to you, All-seer:
release me, Sakyan, from my indecisions.”
The Questions of Dhotaka (Snp 5.6 4.1)

“I am not able to release anyone
in the world who is indecisive, Dhotaka.
But when you understand the best of teachings,
you shall cross this flood.”
The Questions of Dhotaka (Snp 5.6 5.1)

“Teach me, brahmin, out of compassion,
the principle of seclusion so that I may understand.
I wish to practice right here, peaceful, independent,
unobstructed as space itself.”
The Questions of Dhotaka (Snp 5.6 6.1)

“I shall extol that peace for you,” replied the Buddha,
“that is apparent in the present, not relying on legends.
Having understood it, one who lives mindfully
may cross over clinging in the world.”
The Questions of Dhotaka (Snp 5.6 7.1)

“And I rejoice, great seer,
in that supreme peace,
having understood which, one who lives mindfully
may cross over clinging in the world.”
The Questions of Dhotaka (Snp 5.6 8.1)

“Once you have understood that everything,” replied the Buddha,
“you are aware of in the world—
above, below, all round, between—
is a chain, don’t crave for life after life.”
The Questions of Upasīva (Snp 5.7 1.1)

“Alone and independent, O Sakyan,” said Venerable Upasīva,
“I am not able to cross the great flood.
Tell me a support, All-seer,
depending on which I may cross this flood.”
The Questions of Upasīva (Snp 5.7 2.1)

“Mindfully contemplating nothingness,” replied the Buddha,
“depending on the perception ‘there is nothing’, cross the flood.
Giving up sensual pleasures, refraining from chatter,
watch day and night for the ending of craving.”
The Questions of Upasīva (Snp 5.7 3.1)

“One who is free of desire for sensual pleasures,” said Venerable Upasīva,
“depending on nothingness, all else left behind,
freed in the ultimate liberation of perception:
might they remain there without traveling on?”
The Questions of Upasīva (Snp 5.7 4.1)

“One free of desire for sensual pleasures,” replied the Buddha,
“depending on nothingness, all else left behind,
freed in the ultimate liberation of perception:
they might remain there without traveling on.”
The Questions of Upasīva (Snp 5.7 5.1)

“If they were to remain there without traveling on,
even for myriad years, All-seer,
and, being freed, were to grow cool right there,
would the consciousness of that sort pass away?”
The Questions of Upasīva (Snp 5.7 6.1)

“As a flame tossed by a gust of wind,” replied the Buddha,
“comes to an end and cannot be reckoned;
so too, a sage freed from the set of mental phenomena
comes to an end and cannot be reckoned.”
The Questions of Upasīva (Snp 5.7 7.1)

“One who has disappeared—do they not exist?
Or are they free from disease for eternity?
Please, sage, answer me clearly,
for truly you understand this matter.”
The Questions of Upasīva (Snp 5.7 8.1)

“One who has disappeared cannot be defined,” replied the Buddha.
“They have nothing by which others might describe them.
When all things have been eradicated,
eradicated, too, are all ways of speech.”
The Questions of Nanda (Snp 5.8 1.1)

“People say there are sages in the world,” said Venerable Nanda,
“but how is this the case?
Is someone called a sage because of their knowledge,
or because of their way of life?”
The Questions of Nanda (Snp 5.8 2.1)

“Experts do not speak of a sage in terms of
view, learning, or knowledge.
Those who are sages live far from the crowd, I say,
untroubled, with no need for hope.”
The Questions of Nanda (Snp 5.8 3.1)

“As to those ascetics and brahmins,” said Venerable Nanda,
“who speak of purity in terms of what is seen or heard,
or in terms of precepts and vows,
or in terms of countless different things.
Living self-controlled in that matter,
have they crossed over rebirth and old age, good fellow?
I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this.”
The Questions of Nanda (Snp 5.8 4.1)

“As to those ascetics and brahmins,” replied the Buddha,
“who speak of purity in terms of what is seen or heard,
or in terms of precepts and vows,
or in terms of countless different things.
Even though they live self-controlled in that matter,
they’ve not crossed over rebirth and old age, I declare.”
The Questions of Nanda (Snp 5.8 5.1)

“As to those ascetics and brahmins,” said Venerable Nanda,
“who speak of purity in terms of what is seen or heard,
or in terms of precepts and vows,
or in terms of countless different things.
You say they have not crossed the flood, sage.
So who then in the world of gods and humans
has crossed over rebirth and old age, good fellow?
I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this.”
The Questions of Nanda (Snp 5.8 6.1)

“I don’t say that all ascetics and brahmins,” replied the Buddha,
“are shrouded by rebirth and old age.
There are those here who have given up all
that is seen, heard, and thought, and precepts and vows,
who have given up all the countless different things.
Fully understanding craving, they are free of defilements,
those people, I say, have crossed the flood.”
The Questions of Nanda (Snp 5.8 7.1)

“I rejoice in the words of the great seer!
You have expounded non-attachment well, Gotama.
There are those here who have given up all
that is seen, heard, and thought, and precepts and vows,
who have given up all the countless different things.
Fully understanding craving, they are free of defilements,
those people, I agree, have crossed the flood.”
The Questions of Hemaka (Snp 5.9 1.1)

“Those who have previously answered me,” said Venerable Hemaka,
“before Gotama’s teaching,
said ‘thus it was’ or ‘so it shall be’.
All that was just the testament of hearsay;
all that just fostered speculation:
I found no delight in that.
The Questions of Hemaka (Snp 5.9 2.1)

But you, sage, explain to me
the teaching that destroys craving.
Having understood it, one who lives mindfully
may cross over clinging in the world.”
The Questions of Hemaka (Snp 5.9 3.1)

“The removal of desire and lust, Hemaka,
for pleasant things
seen, heard, thought, or cognized here
is extinguishment, the state that does not pass.
The Questions of Hemaka (Snp 5.9 4.1)

Those who have fully understood this, mindful,
are quenched in this very life.
Always at peace,
they’ve crossed over clinging to the world.”
The Questions of Todeyya (Snp 5.10 1.1)

“In whom sensual pleasures do not dwell,” said Venerable Todeyya,
“and for whom there is no craving,
and who has crossed over indecision—
of what kind is their liberation?”
The Questions of Todeyya (Snp 5.10 2.1)

“In whom sensual pleasures do not dwell,” replied the Buddha,
“and for whom there is no craving,
and who has crossed over indecision—
there is no liberation that is further.”
The Questions of Todeyya (Snp 5.10 3.1)

“Are they free of hope, or are they still in need of hope?
Do they possess wisdom, or are they still forming wisdom?
O Sakyan, elucidate the sage to me,
so that I may understand, All-seer.”
The Questions of Todeyya (Snp 5.10 4.1)

“They are free of hope, they are not in need of hope.
They possess wisdom, they are not still forming wisdom.
That, Todeyya, is how to understand a sage,
one who has nothing, unattached to sensual life.”
The Questions of Kappa (Snp 5.11 1.1)

“For those overwhelmed by old age and death,” said Venerable Kappa,
“stuck mid-stream
as the terrifying flood arises,
tell me an island, good fellow.
Explain to me an island
so this may occur no further.”
The Questions of Kappa (Snp 5.11 2.1)

“For those overwhelmed by old age and death,” replied the Buddha,
“stuck mid-stream
as the terrifying flood arises,
I shall tell you an island, Kappa.
The Questions of Kappa (Snp 5.11 3.1)

Having nothing, taking nothing:
this is the island with nothing further.
I call it extinguishment,
the ending of old age and death.
The Questions of Kappa (Snp 5.11 4.1)

Those who have fully understood this, mindful,
are quenched in this very life.
They don’t fall under Māra’s sway,
nor are they his footmen.”
The Questions of Jatukaṇṇī (Snp 5.12 1.1)

“Hearing of the hero with no desire for sensual pleasures,” said Venerable Jatukaṇṇī,
“who has passed over the flood, I’ve come with a question for that desireless one.
Tell me the state of peace, O natural visionary.
Tell me this, Blessed One, as it really is.
The Questions of Jatukaṇṇī (Snp 5.12 2.1)

For, having mastered sensual desires, the Blessed One proceeds,
as the blazing sun shines on the earth.
May you of vast wisdom explain the teaching
to me of little wisdom so that I may understand
the giving up of rebirth and old age here.”
The Questions of Jatukaṇṇī (Snp 5.12 3.1)

“With desire for sensual pleasures dispelled,” replied the Buddha,
“seeing renunciation as sanctuary,
don’t be taking up or putting down
anything at all.
The Questions of Jatukaṇṇī (Snp 5.12 4.1)

What came before, let wither away,
and after, let there be nothing.
If you don’t grasp at the middle,
you will live at peace.
The Questions of Jatukaṇṇī (Snp 5.12 5.1)

One rid of greed, brahmin,
for the whole realm of name and form,
has no defilements by which
they might fall under the sway of Death.”
The Questions of Bhadrāvudha (Snp 5.13 1.1)

“I beseech you, the bastion-leaver, the craving-cutter, the imperturbable,” said Venerable Bhadrāvudha,
“the delight-leaver, the flood-crosser, the freed,
the formulation-leaver, the intelligent.
Different people have gathered from across the nations
The Questions of Bhadrāvudha (Snp 5.13 2.1)

wishing to hear your word, O hero.
After hearing the spiritual giant they will depart from here.
Please, sage, answer them clearly,
for truly you understand this matter.”
The Questions of Bhadrāvudha (Snp 5.13 3.1)

“Dispel all craving for attachments,” replied the Buddha,
“above, below, all round, between.
For whatever a personage grasps in the world,
Māra pursues them right there.
The Questions of Bhadrāvudha (Snp 5.13 4.1)

So let a mindful mendicant who understands
not grasp anything in all the world,
observing that, in clinging to attachments,
these people cling to the domain of death.”
The Questions of Udaya (Snp 5.14 1.1)

“To the meditator, rid of hopes,” said Venerable Udaya,
“who has completed the task, is free of defilements,
and has gone beyond all things,
I have come seeking with a question.
Tell me the liberation by enlightenment,
the smashing of ignorance.”
The Questions of Udaya (Snp 5.14 2.1)
The Questions of Udaya (Snp 5.14 3.1)

pure equanimity and mindfulness,
preceded by investigation of principles—
this, I declare, is liberation by enlightenment,
the smashing of ignorance.”
The Questions of Udaya (Snp 5.14 4.1)

“What fetters the world?
How does it travel about?
With the giving up of what
is extinguishment spoken of?”
The Questions of Udaya (Snp 5.14 5.1)

“Delight fetters the world.
It travels about by means of thought.
With the giving up of craving
extinguishment is spoken of.”
The Questions of Udaya (Snp 5.14 6.1)

“For one living mindfully,
how does consciousness cease?
We’ve come to ask the worthy sir:
let us hear what you say.”
The Questions of Udaya (Snp 5.14 7.1)

“Not taking pleasure in feeling
internally and externally—
for one living mindfully,
that’s how consciousness ceases.”
The Question of Posāla (Snp 5.15 1.1)

“To the one who reveals the past,” said Venerable Posāla,
“who is imperturbable, with doubts cut off,
and who has gone beyond all things,
I have come seeking with a question.
The Question of Posāla (Snp 5.15 2.1)

Consider one who perceives that form has vanished,
who has entirely given up the body,
and who sees nothing at all
internally and externally.
I ask the Sakyan about knowledge for them;
how should that sort be guided?”
The Question of Posāla (Snp 5.15 3.1)

“The Realized One directly knows,” said the Buddha,
“all planes of consciousness.
And he knows this one who remains,
committed to that as their final goal.
The Question of Posāla (Snp 5.15 4.1)

Understanding that desire for rebirth
in the dimension of nothingness is a fetter,
and directly knowing what this really means,
one then discerns that matter clearly.
That is their knowledge of truth,
the brahmin who has lived the life.”
The Questions of Mogharāja (Snp 5.16 1.1)

“Twice I have asked the Sakyan,” said Venerable Mogharāja,
“but you haven’t answered me, O Clear-eyed One.
I have heard that the divine seer
answers when questioned a third time.
The Questions of Mogharāja (Snp 5.16 2.1)

Regarding this world, the other world,
and the realm of divinity with its gods,
I’m not familiar with the view
of the renowned Gotama.
The Questions of Mogharāja (Snp 5.16 3.1)

So I have come seeking with a question
for the one of excellent vision.
How to look upon the world
so the King of Death won’t see you?”
The Questions of Mogharāja (Snp 5.16 4.1)

“Look upon the world as empty,
Mogharāja, ever mindful.
Having uprooted the theory of self,
you may thus cross over death.
That’s how to look upon the world
so the King of Death won’t see you.”
The Questions of Piṅgiya (Snp 5.17 1.1)

“I am old, feeble, and pallid,” said Venerable Piṅgiya,
“my eyes unclear, my hearing faint—
don’t let me perish while still confused.
Explain the teaching so that I may understand
the giving up of rebirth and old age here.”
The Questions of Piṅgiya (Snp 5.17 2.1)

“Seeing them being harmed on account of forms,” replied the Buddha,
“those negligent folk are inflicted on account of forms—
therefore, Piṅgiya, being diligent,
give up form so as not to be reborn.”
The Questions of Piṅgiya (Snp 5.17 3.1)

“The four quarters, the intermediate directions,
below, and above: in these ten directions
there’s nothing at all in the world
that you’ve not seen, heard, thought, or cognized.
Explain the teaching so that I may understand
the giving up of rebirth and old age here.”
The Questions of Piṅgiya (Snp 5.17 4.1)

“Observing mankind sunk in craving,” replied the Buddha,
“tormented, mired in old age;
therefore, Piṅgiya, being diligent,
give up craving so as not to be reborn.”
Homage to the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.18 1.1)

This was said by the Buddha while staying in the land of the Magadhans at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine. When requested by the sixteen brahmin devotees, he answered their questions one by one. If you understand the meaning and the teaching of each of these questions, and practice in line with the teaching, you may go right to the far shore of old age and death. These teachings are said to lead to the far shore, which is why the name of this exposition of the teaching is “The Way to the Far Shore”.
Homage to the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.18 2.1)

Ajita, Tissametteyya,
Puṇṇaka and Mettagū,
Dhotaka and Upasiva,
Nanda and then Hemaka,
Homage to the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.18 3.1)

both Todeyya and Kappa,
and Jatukaṇṇī the astute,
Bhadrāvudha and Udaya,
and the brahmin Posāla,
Mogharāja the intelligent,
and Piṅgiya the great seer:
Homage to the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.18 4.1)

they approached the Buddha,
the seer of consummate conduct.
Asking their subtle questions,
they came to the most excellent Buddha.
Homage to the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.18 5.1)

The Buddha answered their questions
in accordance with truth.
The sage satisfied the brahmins
with his answers to their questions.
Homage to the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.18 6.1)

Those who were satisfied by the Clear-eyed One,
the Buddha, Kinsman of the Sun,
led the spiritual life in his presence,
the one of such outstanding wisdom.
Homage to the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.18 7.1)

If you practice in accordance
with each of these questions
as taught by the Buddha,
you’ll go from the near shore to the far.
Homage to the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.18 8.1)

Developing the supreme path,
you’ll go from the near shore to the far.
This path is for going to the far shore;
that’s why it’s called “The Way to the Far Shore”.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 1.1)

“I shall keep reciting the Way to the Far Shore,” said Venerable Piṅgiya,
“which was taught as it was seen
by the immaculate one of vast intelligence.
He is desireless, unentangled, a spiritual giant:
why would he speak falsely?
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 2.1)

Come, let me extol
in sweet words of praise
the one who’s given up stains and delusions,
conceit and contempt.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 3.1)

The Buddha, All-seer, dispeller of darkness,
has gone to world’s end, beyond all rebirths;
he is free of defilements, and has given up all suffering,
the rightly-named one, brahmin, is revered by me.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 4.1)

Like a bird that flees a little copse,
to roost in a forest abounding in fruit,
I’ve left the near-sighted behind,
like a swan come to a great river.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 5.1)

Those who explained to me previously,
before Gotama’s teaching,
said ‘thus it was’ or ‘so it shall be’.
All that was just the testament of hearsay;
all that just fostered speculation.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 6.1)

Alone, the dispeller of darkness
is brilliant, a beacon:
Gotama, vast in wisdom,
Gotama, vast in intelligence.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 7.1)

He is the one who taught me Dhamma,
apparent in the present life, immediately effective,
the untroubled, the end of craving,
to which there is no compare.”
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 8.1)

“Why would you dwell apart from him
even for an hour, Piṅgiya?
From Gotama, vast in wisdom,
from Gotama, vast in intelligence?
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 9.1)

He is the one who taught you Dhamma,
apparent in the present life, immediately effective,
the untroubled, the end of craving,
to which there is no compare.”
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 10.1)

“I never dwell apart from him,
not even for an hour, brahmin.
From Gotama, vast in wisdom,
from Gotama, vast in intelligence.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 11.1)

He is the one who taught me Dhamma,
apparent in the present life, immediately effective,
the untroubled, the end of craving,
to which there is no compare.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 12.1)

Being diligent, I see him
in my mind’s eye day and night.
I spend the night in homage to him,
hence I think I dwell with him.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 13.1)

My faith and joy and intent and mindfulness
never stray from Gotama’s teaching.
I bow to whatever direction
the one of vast wisdom heads.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 14.1)

I’m old and feeble,
so my body cannot go there,
but I always travel in my thoughts,
for my mind, brahmin, is bound to him.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 15.1)

Lying floundering in the mud,
I drifted from island to island.
Then I saw the Buddha,
the undefiled one who has crossed the flood.”
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 16.1)

“Just as Vakkali was committed to faith—
Bhadrāvudha and Gotama of Āḷavī too—
so too you should commit to faith.
You will go, Piṅgiya, beyond the domain of death.”
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 17.1)

“My confidence grows
as I hear the word of the sage,
the Buddha with veil cast off,
so kind and eloquent.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 18.1)

Having directly known all about the gods,
he understands all top to bottom,
the Teacher who settles all questions
for those who admit their doubts.
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 19.1)

The unfaltering, the unshakable:
that to which there is no compare.
For sure I will go there, I have no doubt of that.
Remember me as one whose mind is made up.”
Preserving the Way to the Far Shore (Snp 5.19 40.5)
The Anthology of Discourses is completed.
Subhūti (Thag 1.1 1.0.2)
Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!
Subhūti (Thag 1.1 1.1)

Like the lions of mighty fang
who roar in mountain caves—
hear now from those who’ve practiced well
their own verses about themselves.
Subhūti (Thag 1.1 2.1)

What their name, and what their clan,
and how they lived by the teaching;
how dedicated were those wise ones,
as they meditated tirelessly.
Subhūti (Thag 1.1 3.1)

Clearly discerning in every case,
they reached the state that does not pass.
Reviewing their completed task,
they spoke about it in these words.
Subhūti (Thag 1.1 4.1)

My hut is roofed and pleasant, sheltered from the wind:
so rain, heavens, as you please!
My mind is serene and freed,
I practice wholeheartedly: so rain, heavens!
Subhūti (Thag 1.1 4.5)
That is how this verse was recited by the senior venerable Subhūti.
Mahākoṭṭhita (Thag 1.2 1.1)

Calm and still,
thoughtful in counsel, not restless—
he shakes off bad qualities
as the gale shakes leaves off a tree.
Mahākoṭṭhita (Thag 1.2 1.5)
That is how this verse was recited by the senior venerable Mahākoṭṭhita.
Revata the Doubter (Thag 1.3 1.1)

See this wisdom of the Realized Ones!
Like a fire blazing in the night,
giving light, giving vision,
they dispel the doubt of those who’ve come.
Revata the Doubter (Thag 1.3 1.5)
That is how this verse was recited by the senior venerable Revata the Doubter.
Puṇṇa (1st) (Thag 1.4 1.1)

Associate only with the virtuous,
the astute ones who see the goal.
The attentive ones, diligent and clear-seeing,
realize the goal
so great and profound,
hard to see, subtle, and very fine.
Puṇṇa (1st) (Thag 1.4 1.7)
That is how this verse was recited by the senior venerable Puṇṇa son of Mantāṇī.
Dabba (Thag 1.5 1.1)
Dabba (Thag 1.5 1.5)
That is how this verse was recited by the senior venerable Dabba.
Sītavaniya (Thag 1.6 1.1)

The monk who went to the Cool Grove is solitary,
content and serene,
victorious, with goosebumps vanished,
guarding mindfulness of the body, steadfast.
Sītavaniya (Thag 1.6 1.5)
That is how this verse was recited by the senior venerable Sītavaniya.
Bhalliya (Thag 1.7 1.1)

He has cast aside the army of the King of Death,
as a fragile bridge of reeds by a great flood.
Victorious since his fears have vanished:
tame and steadfast, he has become quenched.
Bhalliya (Thag 1.7 1.5)
That is how this verse was recited by the senior venerable Bhalliya.
Vīra (Thag 1.8 1.1)
Vīra (Thag 1.8 1.5)
That is how this verse was recited by the senior venerable Vīra.
Pilindavaccha (Thag 1.9 1.1)

It was welcome, not unwelcome,
the advice I got was good.
Of the well-explained teachings,
I arrived at the best.
Pilindavaccha (Thag 1.9 1.5)
That is how this verse was recited by the senior venerable Pilindavaccha.
Puṇṇamāsa (1st) (Thag 1.10 1.1)

A knowledge master, peaceful and self-controlled,
is rid of concern for this world and the world beyond.
Unsullied in the midst of all things,
they’d know the arising and passing of the world.
Puṇṇamāsa (1st) (Thag 1.10 1.5)
That is how this verse was recited by the senior venerable Puṇṇamāsa.
Cūḷavaccha (Thag 1.11 1.1)

A monk full of joy
in the teaching proclaimed by the Buddha
would realize the peaceful state,
the blissful stilling of conditions.
Mahāvaccha (Thag 1.12 1.1)

Empowered by wisdom, with precepts and observances intact,
serene, loving absorption, mindful,
eating just the needed food,
one should await one’s time here, free of desire.
Vanavaccha (1st) (Thag 1.13 1.1)

Glistening, they look like blue stormclouds,
with waters cool and streams so clear,
and covered all in ladybugs:
these rocky crags delight me!
The Novice Sivaka (Thag 1.14 1.1)

My mentor said to me:
“Let’s leave here, Sīvaka.”
My body lives in the village,
but my mind has gone to the wilderness.
I go there even when lying down—
you can’t chain those who know.
Kuṇḍadhāna (Thag 1.15 1.1)

Five to cut, five to drop,
and five more to develop.
When a mendicant slips five chains
they’re said to have crossed the flood.
Belaṭṭhasīsa (Thag 1.16 1.1)

Just as a fine thoroughbred
proceeds with ease,
tail and mane flying in the wind;
so my days and nights
proceed with ease,
full of joy not of the flesh.
Dāsaka (Thag 1.17 1.1)

One who gets drowsy from overeating,
fond of sleep, rolling round the bed
like a great hog stuffed with grain:
that dullard returns to the womb again and again.
Sigāla’s Father (Thag 1.18 1.1)

There was an heir of the Buddha,
a monk in Bhesakaḷā forest,
who suffused the entire earth
with the perception of bones.
I think he will quickly
get rid of sensual desire.
Kula (Thag 1.19 1.1)

While irrigators guide water,
fletchers bend arrows straight,
and carpenters bend timber straight,
those true to their vows tame themselves.
Ajita (Thag 1.20 1.1)

I do not fear death;
nor do I long for life.
I’ll lay down this body,
aware and mindful.
Nigrodha (Thag 1.21 1.1)

I’m not afraid of fear,
for our teacher is expert in freedom from death.
Mendicants advance by the path
where no fear remains.
Cittaka (Thag 1.22 1.1)

Crested peacocks with beautiful blue necks
cry out in Karaṁvī.
Stirred by a cool breeze,
they wake the sleeper to practice absorption.
Gosāla (Thag 1.23 1.1)

I’ll eat honey and milk-rice
in Veḷugumba.
And then, dexterously probing
the rise and fall of the aggregates,
I’ll return to my forest hill
and foster seclusion.
Sugandha (Thag 1.24 1.1)

See the excellence of the teaching!
Just one rainy season after I went forth,
I attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
Nandiya (Thag 1.25 1.1)

Dark One, after attacking such a monk—
one who has arrived at the fruit,
and whose mind is always full of light—
you’ll fall into suffering.
Abhaya (Thag 1.26 1.1)

Having heard the fine words
of the Buddha, Kinsman of the Sun,
I penetrated the subtle truth,
like a hair-tip with an arrow.
Lomasakaṅgiya (Thag 1.27 1.1)

With my chest I’ll thrust aside
the grasses, vines, canes,
the vetiver, rushes and reeds,
and foster seclusion.
Jambugāmikaputta (Thag 1.28 1.1)

Aren’t you obsessed with clothes?
Don’t you just love jewelry?
Is it not you—and no one else—
who spreads the scent of virtue?
Hārita (1st) (Thag 1.29 1.1)

Straighten yourself,
like a fletcher an arrow.
When your mind is upright, Hārita,
break ignorance to bits!
Uttiya (1st) (Thag 1.30 1.1)

When I was ill in the past,
mindfulness arose in me.
Now I am ill once more—
it’s time for me to be heedful.
Gahvaratīriya (Thag 1.31 1.1)

Pestered by flies and mosquitoes
in the wilds, the formidable forest,
one should mindfully endure,
like an elephant at the head of the battle.
Suppiya (Thag 1.32 1.1)

I’ll swap old age for the unaging,
burning for quenching—
the ultimate peace,
the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
Sopāka (1st) (Thag 1.33 1.1)

Just as a mother would be good
to her beloved only child;
so, to creatures all and everywhere,
let one be good.
Posiya (Thag 1.34 1.1)

It’s always better for a smart person
to avoid sharing a seat with such women.
I went from the village to the wilderness;
from there I entered a house.
Though I was there to be fed,
I got up and left without taking leave.
Sāmaññakāni (Thag 1.35 1.1)

Seeking happiness, they find it through this practice.
They get a good reputation and grow in fame,
those who develop the direct route:
the noble eightfold path to realize freedom from death.
Kumāputta (Thag 1.36 1.1)

Learning is good, living well is good,
the life without abode is always good.
Questions on the meaning, actions that are skillful:
this is the ascetic life for one who has nothing.
Kumāputtasahāyaka (Thag 1.37 1.1)

Some travel to different countries,
wandering undisciplined.
If they lose their meditation,
what will such rotten conduct achieve?
So you should dispel aggression,
practicing absorption undistracted.
Gavampati (Thag 1.38 1.1)

His psychic power made the Sarabhū River stand still;
Gavampati is unbound and unperturbed.
The gods bow to that great sage, who has slipped all chains,
and gone beyond rebirth.
Tissa (1st) (Thag 1.39 1.1)

Like they’re struck by a sword,
like their head was on fire,
a mendicant should wander mindful
to give up sensual desire.
Vaḍḍhamāna (Thag 1.40 1.1)

Like they’re struck by a sword,
like their head was on fire,
a mendicant should wander mindful,
to give up desire for rebirth.
Sirivaḍḍha (Thag 1.41 1.1)

Lightning flashes down
on the cleft of Vebhāra and Paṇḍava.
But in the mountain cleft he is absorbed in jhāna—
the son of the Buddha, inimitable and unaffected.
Revata of the Acacia Wood (Thag 1.42 1.1)

Cālā, Upacālā, Sīsupacālā—
meditate mindfully!
I’ve come to you like a hair-splitter.
Sumaṅgala (Thag 1.43 1.1)

Well freed! Well freed!
I’m very well freed from three crooked things:
my sickles, my ploughs,
and my little hoes.
Even if they were here, right here—
I’d be done with them, done!
Practice absorption Sumaṅgala! Practice absorption Sumaṅgala!
Stay heedful, Sumaṅgala!
Sānu (Thag 1.44 1.1)

Mum, they weep for the dead,
or for one who’s alive but missing.
I’m alive and you can see me,
so mum, why do you weep for me?
Ramaṇīyavihārin (Thag 1.45 1.1)

Though a fine thoroughbred may stumble,
it soon stands firm again.
Even so is one accomplished in vision,
a disciple of the Buddha.
Samiddhi (Thag 1.46 1.1)

I went forth out of faith
from the lay life to homelessness.
My mindfulness and wisdom have grown,
my mind is serene.
Make whatever illusions you want,
it doesn’t bother me.
Ujjaya (Thag 1.47 1.1)

Homage to you, O Buddha, O hero,
freed in every way!
Meditating in the fruits of your practice,
I live without defilements.
Sañjaya (Thag 1.48 1.1)

Since I went forth
from the lay life to homelessness,
I’ve not been aware of any thought
that is ignoble and hateful.
Rāmaṇeyyaka (Thag 1.49 1.1)

Even with all the sounds,
the chirping and cheeping of the birds,
my mind doesn’t flounder,
for I’m devoted to oneness.
Vimala (1st) (Thag 1.50 1.1)

The celestial lake Dharaṇī pours, the heavenly gale blows,
and lightning flashes across the sky!
But my thoughts are stilled,
my mind is serene.
Godhika (Thag 1.51 1.1)

The heavens rain like a sweet song;
my hut is roofed and pleasant, sheltered from the wind.
My mind is serene:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.
Subāhu (Thag 1.52 1.1)

The heavens rain like a sweet song;
my hut is roofed and pleasant, sheltered from the wind.
My mind is immersed in my body:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.
Valliya (1st) (Thag 1.53 1.1)

The heavens rain like a sweet song;
my hut is roofed and pleasant, sheltered from the wind.
I meditate there, diligent:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.
Uttiya (2nd) (Thag 1.54 1.1)

The heavens rain like a sweet song;
my hut is roofed and pleasant, sheltered from the wind.
I dwell there without a partner:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.
Añjanavaniya (Thag 1.55 1.1)

I plunged into the Añjana wood
and made a hut to live in.
I’ve attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
Kuṭivihārin (1st) (Thag 1.56 1.1)

“Who is in this hut?” “A monk is in this hut,
free of lust, his mind serene.
Reverend, you should know this:
your hut wasn’t built in vain.”
Kuṭivihārin (2nd) (Thag 1.57 1.1)

This was your old hut,
but you still want a new hut.
Let go of hope for a hut, monk!
A new hut will only bring more suffering.
Ramaṇīyakuṭika (Thag 1.58 1.1)

My hut is pleasing, delightful,
a gift given in faith.
I’ve no need of girls:
go, ladies, to those in need!
Kosalavihārin (Thag 1.59 1.1)

I went forth out of faith
and built a hut in the wilderness.
I’m heedful, ardent,
aware, and mindful.
Sīvali (Thag 1.60 1.1)

My wishes—the purpose I had
for entering this hut—came true.
Seeking knowledge and liberation,
I gave up the tendency to conceit.
Vappa (Thag 1.61 1.1)

One who sees
sees those who see and those who don’t.
One who doesn’t see
sees neither.
Vajjiputta (1st) (Thag 1.62 1.1)

We dwell alone in the wilderness,
like a log dumped in a forest.
Lots of people are jealous of me,
as beings in hell are of one going to heaven.
Pakkha (Thag 1.63 1.1)

They fall, collapsed and fallen;
greedy, they return.
The work is done, the joyful is enjoyed,
happiness is found through happiness.
Vimalakoṇḍañña (Thag 1.64 1.1)

I arose from the one named after a tree;
I was born of the one whose banner shines.
The banner killer has destroyed the great banner,
by means of the banner itself.
Ukkhepakatavaccha (Thag 1.65 1.1)

Vaccha has tossed away
what he built over many years.
Sitting comfortably, uplifted with joy,
he teaches this to householders.
Meghiya (Thag 1.66 1.1)

He counseled me, the great hero,
the one who has gone beyond all things.
When I heard his teaching
I stayed close by him, mindful.
I’ve attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
Ekadhammasavanīya (Thag 1.67 1.1)

My defilements have been burnt away by practicing absorption—
rebirth into all states of existence is eradicated,
transmigration through births is finished,
now there’ll be no more future lives.
Ekudāniya (Thag 1.68 1.1)

A sage of higher consciousness, diligent,
training in the ways of sagacity:
there are no sorrows for the unaffected,
calm and ever mindful.
Channa (Thag 1.69 1.1)

Hearing the sweet Dhamma taught by the master,
all-knowing, of superb knowledge,
I’ve entered the path to realize freedom from death—
he is the expert on the road to sanctuary from the yoke.
Puṇṇa (2nd) (Thag 1.70 1.1)

Ethical conduct is best in this life,
but one with wisdom is supreme.
Someone with both virtue and wisdom
is victorious among men and gods.
Vacchapāla (Thag 1.71 1.1)
Ātuma (Thag 1.72 1.1)

A young bamboo is hard to extract
when the point is grown and become all woody.
That’s how I feel with the wife who was arranged for me.
Give me permission—now I’ve gone forth.
Māṇava (Thag 1.73 1.1)

Seeing an old person, and one suffering from disease,
and a corpse come to the end of life,
I went forth, becoming a wanderer,
and giving up the pleasures of the senses.
Suyāmana (Thag 1.74 1.1)

Sensual desire, ill will,
dullness and drowsiness,
restlessness, and doubt
are not found in a monk at all.
Susārada (Thag 1.75 1.1)

Good is the sight of those who’ve practiced well:
doubt is cut off and intelligence grows—
even a fool grows wise!
That’s why it’s good to meet good people.
Piyañjaha (Thag 1.76 1.1)
Hatthārohaputta (Thag 1.77 1.1)

In the past my mind wandered
how it wished, where it liked, as it pleased.
Now I’ll carefully guide it,
as a trainer with a hook guides a rutting elephant.
Meṇḍasira (Thag 1.78 1.1)

Transmigrating through countless rebirths,
I’ve journeyed without reward.
I’ve suffered, but now
the mass of suffering has fallen away.
Rakkhita (Thag 1.79 1.1)

All my lust is given up,
all my hate is eradicated,
all my delusion is gone:
I’m cooled, quenched.
Ugga (Thag 1.80 1.1)

Any deeds I have done,
a little or a lot,
are all completely exhausted:
now there’ll be no more future lives.
Samitigutta (Thag 1.81 1.1)

Any bad things I’ve done
in previous lives,
are to be experienced right here,
not in any other place.
Kassapa (Thag 1.82 1.1)

Go, child, to any place
where there’s plenty of food,
where it’s safe and free of peril—
may you not be overcome by sorrow!
Sīha (Thag 1.83 1.1)

Meditate diligently, Sīha,
tireless all day and night.
Develop skillful qualities,
and quickly discard this bag of bones.
Nīta (Thag 1.84 1.1)

Sleeping all night,
happily socializing by day,
when will the simpleton
make an end of suffering?
Sunāga (Thag 1.85 1.1)

Skilled in the patterns of the mind,
understanding the nectar of seclusion,
practicing absorption, alert, mindful:
such a person would realize pleasure not of the flesh.
Nāgita (Thag 1.86 1.1)
Paviṭṭha (Thag 1.87 1.1)
Ajjuna (Thag 1.88 1.1)

I was able to lift myself up
from the water to the shore.
While being swept away by the great flood,
I penetrated the truths.
Devasabha (1st) (Thag 1.89 1.1)

I’ve crossed the bogs,
I’ve avoided the chasms,
I’m freed from floods and ties,
and I’ve wiped out all conceit.
Sāmidatta (Thag 1.90 1.1)

The five aggregates are fully understood;
they remain, but their root is cut.
Transmigration through births is finished,
now there’ll be no more future lives.
Paripuṇṇaka (Thag 1.91 1.1)

What I consumed today is considered better
than delicious grain of a hundred flavors—
the Dhamma taught by the Buddha,
Gotama of infinite vision.
Vijaya (Thag 1.92 1.1)
Eraka (Thag 1.93 1.1)

Sensual pleasures are suffering, Eraka!
Sensual pleasures aren’t happiness, Eraka!
One who enjoys sensual pleasures
enjoys suffering, Eraka!
One who doesn’t enjoy sensual pleasures
doesn’t enjoy suffering, Eraka!
Mettaji (Thag 1.94 1.1)

Homage to that Blessed One,
the glorious Sakyan!
Having reached the best,
he beautifully taught the best teaching.
Cakkhupāla (Thag 1.95 1.1)

I’m blind, my eyes are ruined,
I’m traveling a desolate road.
Even if I have to crawl I’ll keep going—
though not with wicked companions.
Khaṇḍasumana (Thag 1.96 1.1)

I offered a single flower
and then amused myself in heavens
for 800 million years;
with what’s left over I’ve become quenched.
Tissa (2nd) (Thag 1.97 1.1)

Giving up a hundred ounces of bronze,
and a hundred grains of gold,
I took a bowl made of clay:
this is my second initiation.
Abhaya (Thag 1.98 1.1)

When you see a sight, mindfulness is lost
as you focus on a pleasant feature.
Experiencing it with a mind full of desire,
you keep clinging to it.
Your defilements grow,
leading to the root of rebirth.
Uttiya (3rd) (Thag 1.99 1.1)

When you hear a sound, mindfulness is lost
as you focus on a pleasant feature.
Experiencing it with a mind full of desire,
you keep clinging to it.
Your defilements grow,
leading to transmigration.
Devasabha (2nd) (Thag 1.100 1.1)

Accomplished in the four right efforts,
mindfulness meditation is your range;
festooned with the flowers of liberation,
undefiled, you’ll be fully quenched.
Belaṭṭhānika (Thag 1.101 1.1)

He’s given up the household life, but is far from perfect.
Living for his belly, lazy, he uses his snout as a plow,
like a great hog stuffed with grain.
That dullard is reborn again and again.
Setuccha (Thag 1.102 1.1)

Deceived by conceit,
defiled among conditions,
oppressed by gain and loss,
they don’t reach immersion.
Bandhura (Thag 1.103 1.1)

I have no need of this—
I’m happy and satisfied with the sweet teaching.
I’ve drunk the best, the supreme nectar:
I won’t go near poison.
Khitaka (Thag 1.104 1.1)

Hey! My body is light,
full of so much rapture and happiness.
My body feels like it’s floating,
like cotton in a gale.
Malitavambha (Thag 1.105 1.1)

Dissatisfied, one should not stay;
and even if happy, one should leave.
One who sees clearly wouldn’t stay
in a place that was not conducive to the goal.
Suhemanta (Thag 1.106 1.1)

Though the meaning has a hundred facets,
and bears a hundred characteristics,
the simpleton sees only one factor,
while the sage sees a hundred.
Dhammasava (Thag 1.107 1.1)

After investigating, I went forth
from the lay life to homelessness.
I’ve attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
Dhammasavapitu (Thag 1.108 1.1)

At 120 years old
I went forth to homelessness.
I’ve attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
Saṅgharakkhita (Thag 1.109 1.1)

Even on retreat he doesn’t heed the counsel
of the one with supreme compassion for his welfare.
He lives with unrestrained faculties,
like a young deer in the woods.
Usabha (1st) (Thag 1.110 1.1)

The trees on the mountain tops have grown tall,
freshly sprinkled by towering clouds.
For Usabha, who loves seclusion, and who thinks only of wilderness,
goodness flourishes more and more.
Jenta (Thag 1.111 1.1)

Going forth is hard; living at home is hard;
Dhamma is profound; money is hard to come by.
Getting by is difficult for we who accept whatever comes,
so we should always think about impermanence.
Vacchagotta (Thag 1.112 1.1)

I am a master of the three knowledges, I’m a great meditator,
an expert in serenity of heart.
I’ve realized my heart’s goal
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
Vanavaccha (2nd) (Thag 1.113 1.1)

The water’s clear and the rocks are broad,
monkeys and deer are all around;
festooned with dewy moss,
these rocky crags delight me!
Adhimutta (1st) (Thag 1.114 1.1)

Your body is uncomfortably heavy,
and life is running out;
greedy for physical pleasure,
how can you find happiness as an ascetic?
Mahānāma (Thag 1.115 1.1)

By Mount Nesādaka,
with its famous covering
of abundant shrubs and trees,
you’re found deficient.
Pārāsariya (1st) (Thag 1.116 1.1)

I’ve given up the six spheres of sense-contact,
my sense doors are guarded and well restrained;
I’ve ejected the root of gloom
and attained the ending of defilements.
Yasa (Thag 1.117 1.1)

I’m well-anointed and well-dressed,
adorned with all my jewelry.
I’ve attained the three knowledges
and fulfilled the Buddha’s instructions.
Kimbila (1st) (Thag 1.118 1.1)

Old age falls like a curse;
it’s the same body, but it seems like someone else’s.
I remember myself as if I were someone else,
but I’m still the same, I haven’t been away.
Vajjiputta (2nd) (Thag 1.119 1.1)

You’ve left for the jungle, the root of a tree,
having laid extinguishment in your heart.
Meditate, Gotama, don’t be negligent!
What use is this hullabaloo to you?
Isidatta (Thag 1.120 1.1)

The five aggregates are fully understood,
they remain, but their root is cut.
I have reached the end of suffering
and attained the ending of defilements.
Uttara (1st) (Thag 2.1 1.1)

No life is permanent,
and no conditions last forever.
The aggregates are reborn
and pass away, again and again.
Uttara (1st) (Thag 2.1 2.1)

Knowing this danger,
I have no need for another life.
I’ve escaped all sensual pleasures,
and attained the ending of defilements.
Uttara (1st) (Thag 2.1 2.5)
That is how these verses were recited by the senior venerable Uttara.
Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer (Thag 2.2 1.1)

You can’t live by fasting,
but food doesn’t lead to peace of heart.
Seeing how this bag of bones is sustained by food,
I wander, seeking.
Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer (Thag 2.2 2.1)

They know it’s just a swamp,
this homage and veneration in respectable families.
Honor is a subtle dart, hard to extract,
and hard for a reprobate to give up.
Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer (Thag 2.2 2.5)
That is how these verses were recited by the senior venerable Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer.
Valliya (2nd) (Thag 2.3 1.1)

A monkey went up to the little hut
with five doors.
He circles around, knocking
on each door, again and again.
Valliya (2nd) (Thag 2.3 2.1)

Stand still monkey, don’t run!
Things are different now;
you’ve been caught by wisdom—
you won’t go far.
Gaṅgātīriya (Thag 2.4 1.1)

My hut on the bank of the Ganges
is made from three palm leaves.
My alms-bowl is a funeral pot,
my robe is cast-off rags.
Gaṅgātīriya (Thag 2.4 2.1)

In my first two rainy seasons
I spoke only one word.
In my third rainy season
the mass of darkness was shattered.
Ajina (Thag 2.5 1.1)

Even a master of the three knowledges,
undefiled, conqueror of death,
is looked down upon for being unknown
by ignorant fools.
Ajina (Thag 2.5 2.1)

But any individual here
who gets food and drink
is honored by them,
even if they are of bad character.
Meḷajina (Thag 2.6 1.1)

When I heard the Teacher
speaking Dhamma,
I wasn’t aware of any doubt
in the all-knowing, unconquered one,
Meḷajina (Thag 2.6 2.1)

the caravan leader, the great hero,
the most excellent of charioteers.
I have no doubt
in the path or practice.
Rādha (Thag 2.7 1.1)

Just as rain seeps into
a poorly roofed house,
lust seeps into
an undeveloped mind.
Rādha (Thag 2.7 2.1)

Just as rain doesn’t seep into
a well roofed house,
lust doesn’t seep into
a well-developed mind.
Surādha (Thag 2.8 1.1)
Surādha (Thag 2.8 2.1)

I’ve attained the goal
for the sake of which I went forth
from the lay life to homelessness—
the ending of all fetters.
Gotama (1st) (Thag 2.9 1.1)

Sages sleep at ease
when they’re not bound to women.
For the truth is hard to find among them
and one must always be guarded.
Gotama (1st) (Thag 2.9 2.1)

Sensual pleasure, you’ve been slain!
We’re not in your debt any more.
Now we go to extinguishment,
where there is no sorrow.
Vasabha (Thag 2.10 1.1)

First one kills oneself,
then one kills others.
One kills oneself, really dead,
like one who kills birds using a dead bird as a decoy.
Vasabha (Thag 2.10 2.1)

A brahmin’s color is not on the outside;
a brahmin is colored on the inside.
Whoever harbors bad deeds
is truly a dark one, Sujampati.
Mahācunda (Thag 2.11 1.1)
Mahācunda (Thag 2.11 2.1)

You should frequent remote lodgings
and practice to be released from fetters.
If you don’t find enjoyment there,
live in the Saṅgha, self-protected and mindful.
Jotidāsa (Thag 2.12 1.1)

People who act harshly—
attacking people,
binding them with rope,
hurting them in all kinds of ways—
they’re treated in the same way;
their deeds don’t vanish.
Jotidāsa (Thag 2.12 2.1)

Whatever deeds a person does,
whether good or bad,
they are the heir to each
and every deed they do.
Heraññakāni (Thag 2.13 1.1)

The days and nights rush by,
and then life is cut short.
The life of mortals wastes away,
like the water in tiny streams.
Heraññakāni (Thag 2.13 2.1)

But while doing bad deeds
the fool doesn’t realize—
it’ll be bitter later on;
for the result will be bad for them.
Somamitta (Thag 2.14 1.1)

If you’re lost in the middle of a great sea,
and you clamber up on a little log, you’ll sink.
So too, a person who lives well
sinks by relying on a lazy person.
Hence you should avoid such
a lazy person who lacks energy.
Somamitta (Thag 2.14 2.1)

Dwell with the noble ones
who are secluded and determined
and always energetic;
the astute who practice absorption.
Sabbamitta (Thag 2.15 1.1)
Sabbamitta (Thag 2.15 2.1)

So what’s the point of people,
or those born of people?
Go, abandon these people,
who’ve hurt so many people.
Mahākāḷa (Thag 2.16 1.1)
Mahākāḷa (Thag 2.16 2.1)

When an ignorant person builds up attachments,
that dullard returns to suffering again and again.
So let one who understands not build up attachments:
may I never again lie with a broken skull!
Tissa (3rd) (Thag 2.17 1.1)

A shaven one wrapped in the outer robe
gets many enemies
when they receive food and drink,
clothes and bedding.
Tissa (3rd) (Thag 2.17 2.1)

Knowing this danger,
this great fear in honors,
a mendicant should wander mindful,
with few possessions, not festering.
Kimbila (2nd) (Thag 2.18 1.1)

In the Park of the East-Raftered Hall
the Sakyan friends,
having given up great wealth,
are happy with the scraps in their bowls.
Kimbila (2nd) (Thag 2.18 2.1)

Energetic, resolute,
always staunchly vigorous;
having given up mundane delights,
they enjoy the delights of the Dhamma.
Nanda (Thag 2.19 1.1)

Because of focusing on the wrong things,
I was addicted to ornamentation.
I was vain, fickle,
racked by desire for pleasures of the senses.
Nanda (Thag 2.19 2.1)

But with the help of the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun, so skilled in means,
I practiced rationally and extracted
attachment to continued existence from my mind.
Sirima (Thag 2.20 1.1)

If others praise one
who has no immersion,
they praise in vain,
as one has no immersion.
Sirima (Thag 2.20 2.1)

If others criticize one
who does have immersion,
they criticize in vain,
as one does have immersion.
